doc.title: Roscoe Mitchell interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 23, 2023

chapter: Performing and the idea of free jazz
title: Building instruments and working with inventor Steven Sylvester
summary: He encourages building one's own instruments and describes Steven Sylvester's pedal-powered bullroarer and other inventions, and his own constant curiosity.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Yeah, the Baroque flute, that’s right, the Baroque flute I do play that. The entire recorder family, I play that as well. Because I’ve been in several early music groups. So wow, I have a whole collection of instruments that I made that no one even has. Percussion instruments and so on that I play. So there I mean everybody can be an individual because I encourage people that are interested in it, you know, to build their own instrument you know. So that way then everybody has their own instrument. But you know there’s a language that can be created you know with those instruments. So like I — at one time I did a lot of work with Steven Sylvester who is an inventor you know that — he, you know he came to me and he said, “You know what I’m going to do is I’m going to build an instrument that can keep up with you.” And so our first concert was where you know he decided to take a bullroarer, which comes from Australia, you know, and put it on a motor he had at first and then a couple of days before the concert he decided wait a minute, I’m going to put this on pedal power you know. And he put it on pedal power and so when he did that all of a sudden the instrument started to breathe because if you look at somebody who’s riding a bike it looks like that it’s a kind of a smooth thing but it’s not, it’s a breathing spot as that cycle goes around like that. So it started to breathe after that. And I have all of these deals and so on and so forth. I mean you know yeah I mean it’s a big story. Yeah, our last concert with that group, I mean it was in Atlanta. And you know Steven Sylvester, once he put this thing on pedal power I mean he just — his first instrument was a thing where he had the pallet on the side of his head where he’d stuck them up there with some kind of sticky thing and so on. The next one was, it was a long line over the top of his head with triggers in different things so he could let out different sounds and so on. He had these little small metal tubes that he made with slits in them, you know, when they were going fast — ooooo — and when
they were going slow they were hitting each other like little bells and ringing and so on and so forth you know. So yeah, yeah, I mean I learn a lot from him man. You know, really.
You seem to be constantly curious.
Yes. I am. I’m constantly curious. Now even more so than ever. Now even more so than ever.
